paragraphs: This paper examines whether a network that estimates age from a face also develops internal representations capable of distinguishing individual identities. The authors frame that technical question as central to debates about biometric data: processing a facial photograph and possessing a usable identification capability are different things that need to be examined directly.

The paper supplies empirical evidence from 14 models evaluated on three face verification benchmarks. The tested age estimators performed orders of magnitude below identification thresholds. The authors use these results to support their position that age estimation models cannot identify individuals, grounding the argument in measured identification capability rather than the fact that the input contains a face.

The distinction matters because biometric classifications can carry substantial regulatory consequences. The authors call for researchers to disclose what systems retain and what they can actually do, and for regulators to distinguish temporary computation from storing identifying templates. Their contribution connects an empirical capability assessment to a proposal for more technically informed regulation.
icml-2026-position-age-estimation-models.tldr: The authors use face verification evaluations to argue that age estimation should be distinguished from biometric identification.

paragraphs: Evaluating an AI agent often requires adapting it to a benchmark’s particular software setup. The authors argue that these fixed, language-model-centered arrangements create integration work, make testing differ from production use, and complicate comparisons between agents with different designs. They locate the central problem in the absence of a shared assessment interface.

Their proposal, Agentified Agent Assessment, makes the evaluator an agent too. Participants use A2A for managing tasks and MCP for accessing tools. A common interface replaces separate benchmark and agent interfaces, allowing assessment logic to remain independent of how the assessed agent is implemented. This structure is intended to support interoperable, reproducible evaluation, including settings with multiple agents.

The paper also introduces AgentBeats as a concrete realization of this approach. It describes five operating modes that accommodate practical differences in openness, privacy, and reproducibility, together with adoption guidance for developers and benchmark creators. The contribution is an assessment architecture designed to make diverse agents easier to evaluate through common protocols.
icml-2026-position-agent-evaluation-shou.tldr: The paper proposes using evaluator agents and shared protocols to make agent assessment more interoperable and reproducible.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the idea that increasing the scale of a single model is sufficient to reach artificial general intelligence. The authors argue that the varied and complex distribution of real-world tasks calls for agentic systems, and they take the strong position that this organization is a necessary paradigm for mastering that distribution.

The technical argument compares the optimization constraints of a single learner with those of agentic arrangements. It develops from simple routing, which directs work through different components, to general directed acyclic graph structures. Through theoretical derivations, the authors report exponentially better generalization and sample efficiency for agentic AI in their analysis. These are theoretical advantages presented in support of the proposed research direction.

The paper also connects agentic organization to Mixture-of-Experts and offers a reinterpretation of instability in current multi-agent frameworks. Its broader implication is that the organization of learning and computation deserves greater research attention alongside model scale. The work presents agentic AI as a foreseeable route toward AGI, rather than reporting an achieved AGI system.
icml-2026-position-agentic-ai-system-is-.tldr: The authors argue for agentic AI as a necessary pathway toward AGI, supported by theoretical efficiency and generalization advantages.

paragraphs: Street-image assessments combine visible features with judgments about a place. The authors argue that benchmarks for these assessments should preserve human disagreement and decisions not to answer. When outputs inform urban governance, the categories being judged and the rules for scoring answers should also be open to negotiation.

The paper grounds this position in 100 Montreal street scenes assessed along 30 dimensions by 12 participants from seven community organizations. It evaluates seven vision–language models using deterministic zero-shot testing. Across dimensions, model agreement with human consensus varies together with how consistently humans agree with each other. For Overall Impression, model and human response distributions differ, including their rates of selecting Not applicable.

These findings make human reliability part of interpreting model performance. Agreement with a consensus means something different when the people producing that consensus disagree substantially. The authors therefore recommend reporting annotator reliability alongside model alignment and exposing uncertainty and scoring assumptions. Their proposal treats the benchmark as a measurement process whose choices matter to public decisions.
icml-2026-position-benchmarks-for-vision.tldr: Urban perception benchmarks should report human disagreement and abstention and make their categories and scoring rules negotiable.

paragraphs: The paper argues that globally deployed language models expose speakers of low-resource languages to a combination of weaker safety and weaker usefulness. It reports harmful generation rising from 1% in English to 35% in languages such as Hausa, Igbo, and Javanese, alongside a 20-percentage-point decline in instruction following. The authors describe these paired disadvantages as a Dual Curse.

Drawing on a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 207 studies, the authors attribute the disparity to a pre-training bottleneck. They report reward-model accuracy of 49–50% in low-resource languages, around chance, and argue that this makes post-hoc alignment structurally ineffective. They also connect unreliable moderation to governance hazards where automated content moderation is mandated.

Their proposed response combines technical development with community participation. It includes safety context distillation during pre-training, for which the abstract reports 78–89% harm reduction, community involvement in specifying harms, and evaluation that jointly tracks attack resistance and false refusals across languages. This joint assessment matters because blocking harmful requests and preserving legitimate access are both parts of multilingual safety.
icml-2026-position-breaking-the-dual-cur.tldr: The authors argue that multilingual safety requires changes to pre-training, community-defined harms, and evaluation of both harmful responses and false refusals.

paragraphs: Time series forecasting research produces many new neural architectures, yet reported comparisons often disagree. This paper argues that benchmarking practices make those disagreements difficult to resolve because they overlook important differences between the methods being compared. As a result, a performance improvement may be attributed to the wrong design choice.

The authors show that choices commonly treated as implementation details can affect results more than the selection of particular sequence modeling layers. They highlight globality and locality as examples of overlooked dimensions that can change the class of forecasting method and substantially alter empirical performance. Their argument concerns what a comparison actually isolates: an architecture label can conceal consequential differences in how forecasting is organized.

The proposed practical response is an auxiliary forecasting model card. Its fields characterize architectures through key design decisions, making those decisions explicit when introducing or comparing models. The broader recommendation is to organize benchmarking around the foundations of the forecasting problem so that observed gains provide clearer evidence about which components are responsible.
icml-2026-position-current-benchmarking-.tldr: Forecasting comparisons should expose foundational design choices that can influence performance more than the advertised sequence modeling layers.

paragraphs: Explainable AI has produced many techniques for describing model behavior, but the authors argue that those descriptions rarely change real-world workflows. An explanation can be generated successfully and still be discarded without affecting a decision. The paper treats this gap as a problem in how explainability research is formulated and connected to human use.

The authors support their position through an analysis of recent ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR papers and a survey of explainability practitioners. They identify recurring structural issues: unclear problem definitions, evaluation goals that are insufficiently specified, and missing processes for turning explanation-based feedback into changes. These issues limit the field’s ability to build cumulatively toward useful systems.

The paper proposes a practical checklist for making explainability more human-centered and oriented toward action. Its emphasis is on complete workflows in which people inspect explanations, provide feedback, and influence what happens next. The intended shift makes integration and evaluation central research problems, so that progress reflects how explanations support meaningful decisions rather than simply their production.
icml-2026-position-explainability-resear.tldr: Explainability research should clarify its goals and build feedback workflows that turn explanations into useful human action.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing has long dealt with the challenge of combining contributions that vary in quality and consistency. This paper argues that language-model research can benefit from that experience when a model can meaningfully be treated as a worker. The connection covers activities such as producing content, assigning labels, evaluating outputs, and solving problems.

The authors distinguish two directions. In Crowd-LLM-Sourcing, humans and models participate together in a workflow. In LLM-Sourcing inspired by crowdsourcing, established principles for organizing contributions guide work carried out by models. This framing brings quality control and aggregation into a shared discussion instead of treating each use of multiple model contributions as an entirely new problem.

The proposed transfer requires adaptation. Model workers can make correlated errors, and their capabilities depend on context, so mechanisms designed around human workers cannot simply be assumed to behave the same way. The paper’s position is therefore conditional and practical: use crowdsourcing knowledge where the worker analogy fits, while redesigning mechanisms around the distinctive behavior of model-based contributors.
icml-2026-position-from-crowdsourcing-to.tldr: LLM workflows should adapt crowdsourcing principles when models act as workers, accounting for correlated errors and context-dependent abilities.

paragraphs: Interpretability research seeks to explain how deep networks behave, but its practical impact has become a source of concern. This position paper argues that interpretability can support useful action and that evaluation criteria are the central missing ingredient. An insight should be assessed partly by whether it enables decisions or interventions outside interpretability research itself.

The authors define actionable interpretability through two dimensions: concreteness and validation. These dimensions focus attention on whether an insight leads to a specific action and whether its usefulness is supported. They also analyze barriers that keep interpretability work from producing real-world impact, connecting the evaluation problem to the practical use of research findings.

The paper identifies five domains where interpretability can offer distinctive value and proposes a framework whose evaluation criteria track practical outcomes. This is a proposal for making actionability a core research objective, while preserving a place for exploratory work. Its significance is to give researchers a way to connect understanding a model with demonstrating what that understanding allows someone to do.
icml-2026-position-interpretability-can-.tldr: Interpretability should be evaluated by how concretely and credibly its insights enable useful decisions and interventions.

paragraphs: The paper examines why digital services remain difficult to connect despite the Internet’s open foundations. Building interoperable interfaces requires investment, and dominant platforms have limited incentives to make it easier for users to move data elsewhere. The authors argue that language-model agents change these economics by reducing the work needed to connect services.

Agents can translate between data formats and operate interfaces built for people. The paper calls the resulting possibility universal interoperability: digital services exchanging data through adapters mediated by AI. Its central position is that these capabilities make interoperability dramatically cheaper and effectively unavoidable, weakening the dependence on platform owners voluntarily providing open interfaces.

The authors connect this shift to greater data portability, reduced monopolistic behavior, and increased user freedom. They also identify security risks and technical debt as possible consequences of agent-mediated connections. Their recommendation is for the ML community to embrace the development while building frameworks to manage those downsides. The contribution is an argument about how agent capabilities could reshape platform power and integration.
icml-2026-position-llm-agents-are-the-an.tldr: The authors argue that LLM agents can make service interoperability dramatically cheaper while creating security and maintenance challenges.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that current language models remain inadequate for theoretical physics research despite their mathematical and coding abilities. The authors identify shortcomings in physical intuition, satisfaction of constraints, and dependable reasoning. Their claim is that prompting alone cannot close these gaps because useful physics work requires specialized forms of judgment.

The paper emphasizes deciding when approximations are appropriate, exploiting symmetries, and grounding reasoning in physical principles. It proposes agents trained specifically on physics reasoning patterns and supported by verification tools that understand physical requirements. Training and verification serve complementary roles: producing plausible reasoning is only part of the task when theoretical results also need physical consistency.

The authors envision agents that handle multiple data modalities, propose physically consistent hypotheses, and verify theoretical results autonomously. They identify physics-specific datasets, rewards that reflect reasoning quality, and verification frameworks encoding fundamental principles as necessary infrastructure for that vision. This is a research agenda calling for collaboration between physicists and AI researchers, with specialized capabilities and checking mechanisms developed together.
icml-2026-position-llm-for-physics-resea.tldr: The authors argue that useful physics research agents require specialized training and verification tools grounded in physical principles.

paragraphs: Predicting how AI changes work requires understanding more than what models can currently do. The paper frames labor outcomes as an interaction between changing technical capabilities, adoption, organizational restructuring, and political and economic responses. It argues that this makes labor prediction a core scientific problem for the AI and ML community within a broader interdisciplinary effort.

The authors review approaches from economics, management, and machine learning and identify technical obstacles facing existing prediction methods. They connect those obstacles to familiar ML concerns: changing conditions over time, shifts between data distributions, feedback generated within the system being studied, and simulations built from language-model agents. These connections establish a distinctive technical role for ML researchers.

The paper then proposes an agenda for AI- and ML-driven labor prediction. Its contribution is to organize the research problem and explain why capability forecasts alone do not capture how work is reorganized and valued. Progress requires methods that account for adaptation and feedback while drawing on the knowledge of economics and social science.
icml-2026-position-predicting-ais-impact.tldr: Predicting AI’s labor impact is an interdisciplinary ML problem involving changing capabilities, adoption, distribution shifts, and social feedback.

paragraphs: Scientific data often measure proxies for the processes researchers want to understand. A proxy may correlate with several hidden drivers without directly revealing any of them. This paper argues that learning mechanisms from high-dimensional proxies is generally underdetermined: different and incompatible mechanisms can produce essentially the same relationships within the observed data.

That ambiguity changes what successful prediction can establish. A model may predict well and provide a coherent explanation while leaving the underlying mechanism unidentified. The authors argue that AI-generated scientific hypotheses can therefore sound convincing without resolving which process produced the observations. They highlight language models as a particular concern because a fluent account can compress multiple compatible explanations into one narrative.

The paper proposes standards for work described as mechanistic AI. Its central demand is that claims about discovering mechanisms confront the problem of identification, rather than treating predictive performance or explanatory coherence as sufficient evidence. The significance is a clearer boundary between generating plausible scientific hypotheses and establishing which underlying structure the available observations actually support.
icml-2026-position-prioritize-identifyin.tldr: Accurate predictions and persuasive explanations do not establish a mechanism when incompatible mechanisms fit the same observations.

paragraphs: Prompts used in public-sector AI encode roles, ways of framing decisions, and value judgments. The authors argue that these prompts deserve formal governance because changing them can materially change outputs even when model weights and input records stay fixed. Existing documentation and organizational policies rarely make local deployment prompts transparent, contestable, or auditable.

The proposed Prompt Commons is a community-maintained repository of versioned prompt templates. It includes provenance information, licensing, and moderation records so that prompts become artifacts with an inspectable history. This makes the prompt collection itself an object of governance, bringing attention to a layer of deployment that broader model and dataset documentation may overlook.

Using a pilot dataset gathered with community partners in a large North American city, the paper illustrates open, curated, and veto-enabled governance arrangements. The dataset contains 443 human prompts and 3,317 after augmentation. It also illustrates an ensemble method that combines stakeholder prompts into compromise recommendations, then sets out testable implications and an evaluation agenda for governing this layer.
icml-2026-position-prompts-for-public-se.tldr: Public-sector prompts should be versioned, auditable community artifacts because their framing can materially change AI outputs.

paragraphs: This paper argues that AI reasoning research lacks sufficiently shared operational definitions. Although recent progress has largely come from probabilistic generative models, reasoning also has a long history in logic and automated verification. The authors contend that the generative AI community often overlooks that history when deciding what counts as reasoning.

The problem affects evaluation directly. If researchers do not clearly specify the capability a test is meant to measure, they cannot verify that the test actually measures reasoning. The paper describes this as a construct-validity problem and argues that it weakens claims of measurable progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning. Better scores need a clear connection to the capability being claimed.

To address the ambiguity, the authors synthesize existing literature into operational definitions that frame valid and sound reasoning as a learnable process governed by rules. They also provide a checklist for communicating reasoning research. The intended contribution is a common foundation for defining capabilities, interpreting evaluations, and stating research claims with enough precision to assess them.
icml-2026-position-reasoning-is-a-learna.tldr: The paper proposes rule-based operational definitions and reporting practices to make AI reasoning claims meaningfully evaluable.

paragraphs: The paper distinguishes explicit knowledge, such as documentation and databases, from implicit knowledge embedded in reasoning patterns, debugging processes, and intermediate steps. The authors argue that AI absorbs both useful patterns and harmful biases from implicit knowledge. Much of that knowledge remains undocumented because people perceive the cost of recording it as greater than its value.

This creates a verification gap in the authors’ account of AI reliability. Explicit claims can be checked against sources, while reasoning, judgment, and intuition lack similarly inspectable records. The paper argues that reliable AI therefore needs infrastructure that makes this implicit knowledge available for human validation, extending verification beyond already documented facts.

The proposed mechanism is the Knowledge Object: a structured artifact that makes implicit knowledge inspectable, checkable, and endorsable by people. The authors argue that these artifacts change the economics of verification by making previously costly checks feasible. Their envisioned benefit comes from accumulating human validation over time, allowing useful reasoning knowledge to become a resource whose reliability people can actively assess.
icml-2026-position-reliable-ai-needs-to-.tldr: The paper proposes structured Knowledge Objects to make implicit reasoning knowledge available for accumulated human validation.

paragraphs: Some proposals use hidden triggers to activate model behaviors intended to control access, establish ownership, or enforce safety. This paper argues that calling these mechanisms positive backdoors overstates their protective value. It proposes the term Secret Alignment and says security claims should be treated as unestablished unless rigorous, standardized evaluation supports them.

The authors organize these proposals as covert associations between triggers and behaviors. They evaluate three representative applications across effectiveness, harmlessness, persistence, efficiency, robustness, and reliability. Their results reveal substantial brittleness in the mappings, particularly regarding confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The finding challenges whether the intended protective behavior remains dependable under the security demands placed on it.

The paper relates these outcomes to behavior density and decision complexity, offering a behavioral perspective on deployment risks. Its broader context is privately owned language models, where unauthorized access, theft, and misuse create demand for protection. The authors call for community-wide evaluation that can substantiate protective claims, making the burden of evidence central to assessing these hidden mechanisms.
icml-2026-position-retire-the-positive-b.tldr: Evaluations reveal brittle hidden trigger mechanisms, motivating the term Secret Alignment and stronger evidence for protective claims.

paragraphs: A language model can repeatedly generate training material for itself without continuing to improve. This paper identifies a central reason: more synthetic examples may provide no additional information that the next iteration can learn. Through experiments on a self-play coding task, the authors argue that sustained self-evolution requires learnable information to increase across iterations.

They organize the system into three roles. A proposer creates tasks, a solver attempts them, and a verifier supplies training signals. This framing makes improvement a property of the whole data-producing loop. The quantity of generated material alone cannot establish that the tasks, attempted solutions, and feedback jointly create a productive next learning step.

The authors identify three complementary designs: asymmetric co-evolution links weaker and stronger roles; capacity growth increases parameter and inference-time budgets as learnable information rises; and proactive information seeking brings in external context and new task sources. Together, these designs are presented as a measurable route toward sustained improvement. The stated requirement concerns information the system can learn, not simply continued self-play.
icml-2026-position-self-play-only-evolve.tldr: The authors argue that sustained self-improvement requires increasing learnable information across the task-generation, solving, and verification loop.

paragraphs: A model’s leading average benchmark score can support a narrower conclusion than the phrase state of the art suggests. This paper argues that readers often interpret that phrase as meaningful superiority across most tasks. A small gain in an aggregate score, however, does not by itself establish the size, consistency, or stability of that advantage.

The authors analyze ten benchmarks spanning different domains from public leaderboards. In more than half of comparisons between top models, at least one commonly assumed property of superiority fails to hold. These properties include a meaningful effect size, consistency across tasks, and robustness when datasets are removed. Outlier datasets frequently drive aggregate gains, and having many tasks does not eliminate this fragility.

The proposed remedy is to match the language of a claim to what the results establish. The authors emphasize that this can be done without additional experiments, through more accurate reporting of existing evidence. Their contribution is a distinction between winning an aggregate ranking and demonstrating a broader performance advantage that survives closer inspection.
icml-2026-position-state-of-the-art-clai.tldr: Benchmark leadership often fails to establish broad superiority, so state-of-the-art claims should reflect the actual strength of the evidence.

paragraphs: Survival analysis evaluates outcomes in the presence of censoring, where the relevant event information is not fully observed. This paper argues that evaluation practices often overlook how this changes the problem compared with standard regression or classification. Researchers may use metrics that do not match their modeling objective while leaving censoring assumptions implicit or unjustified.

The authors focus especially on concordance-based measures such as the C-index, which they find heavily overused. Their concern is whether the reported score answers the scientific question the model was built to address. They propose criteria for selecting appropriate metrics and a double-helix ladder that links valid evaluation to alignment between metrics and modeling assumptions.

Controlled experiments show that breaking this alignment can produce misleading model comparisons. The paper closes with practical guidance for evaluating survival models. Its message is that a favorable score only has the intended meaning when the measure and its assumptions fit the task; choosing an evaluation method is part of defining a scientifically meaningful comparison.
icml-2026-position-stop-chasing-the-c-in.tldr: Survival-model evaluation should align metrics, modeling goals, and censoring assumptions to avoid misleading comparisons.

paragraphs: Autoformalization converts informal language into a formal language that machines can verify. Much existing work treats an individual statement as the unit of translation. This position paper argues that real formalization operates at a larger scale because a theorem depends on a surrounding network of definitions, assumptions, and supporting results.

The authors propose making complete theories the target of autoformalization. The desired output is a structured library that represents both its constituent statements and their dependencies. This matters because the surrounding mathematical structure is needed before a target theorem can even be expressed formally. Translating an isolated sentence therefore captures only part of the work involved in building formal knowledge.

The paper examines the significance of this change in scope, considers alternative views, identifies open challenges, and proposes three promising research directions. Its contribution is to reframe what an autoformalization system should aim to produce. Success at the theory level would concern an interconnected body of machine-verifiable knowledge, with the relationships between statements treated as part of the formalization task.
icml-2026-position-theory-level-autoform.tldr: Autoformalization should build connected formal theories, including their definitions and dependencies, rather than focus only on individual statements.

paragraphs: An idea developed for one purpose can later become useful for a very different one. The paper uses the biological concept of exaptation to describe this possibility in scientific research. It argues that a research environment dominated by benchmark performance makes it difficult for ideas outside the prevailing evaluation rule to survive long enough to find unexpected uses.

The authors see this pressure as increasingly consequential as AI research asks how intelligent systems can also remain aligned, interpretable, and safe. These questions differ philosophically from asking whether machines can exhibit intelligence. They may require discoveries whose value cannot be specified in advance, making a single dominant selection rule a potential constraint on future progress.

The paper proposes several institutional responses while retaining benchmarking: multiple evaluation regimes, protected venues for work that cannot be directly compared, funding with longer horizons, and training that encourages researchers to question evaluation rules. The aim is to preserve the field’s capacity for unforeseen discoveries by giving ideas room to develop beyond current measures of success.
icml-2026-position-there-are-futures-tha.tldr: The paper argues that AI research needs room for ideas whose future value current benchmarks cannot measure.

paragraphs: Video contains motion, changing states, and information that unfolds across frames. This paper argues that current video-language-model benchmarks can sometimes be solved without reliably perceiving those dynamics. As a result, measured progress can reward answers that sound plausible from language and context without demonstrating that the model used the relevant visual evidence over time.

The authors identify two connected failure modes across recent evaluations. Static-cue dominance occurs when appearance and context outweigh evidence about change. Prior-driven temporal hallucination occurs when learned regularities supply an account of timing or causation, especially when the actual dynamics are subtle or counterintuitive. Both can obscure whether a model follows what happens in the video.

The paper synthesizes diagnostic probes that expose these problems and calls for stronger spatiotemporal grounding in models and benchmarks. The goal is to make evaluation depend on the evidence that video uniquely provides. Its contribution is a diagnosis of how existing assessments can miss dynamic understanding and a research priority centered on motion and state transitions.
icml-2026-position-video-llms-must-not-i.tldr: Video models and benchmarks should require evidence of motion and change, because plausible answers can conceal failures to perceive dynamics.

paragraphs: Different hallucination definitions can make it difficult to compare evaluations or discuss remedies consistently. This paper reviews existing definitions and proposes a unified account: hallucination is inaccurate internal modeling of a world that becomes observable to the user. The relevant world may be represented by a knowledge base or by the source material a model is summarizing.

The framework varies two elements: the reference world model and the policy for deciding what counts as a conflict with it. In this way, it brings earlier definitions into a common structure. A factual statement that contradicts a knowledge base and a summary that contradicts its source can be understood through the same underlying relationship.

The authors argue that this approach makes evaluations specify what reference world they assume and helps distinguish hallucinations from errors in planning or reward. They also connect the framework to HalluWorld, a complementary benchmark with fully specified reference world models. The proposed benefit is clearer comparison and diagnosis, providing shared language for evaluation and mitigation rather than a reported solution to hallucination.
icml-2026-position-we-need-a-unified-def.tldr: The paper unifies hallucination definitions around observable inaccuracies relative to an explicitly chosen reference world model.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization learns from differences between function evaluations without using backpropagation. It attracts interest for memory efficiency and settings with limited access to a system’s internals. This paper challenges the view that noisy estimates and high query costs make it fundamentally unscalable, arguing that many apparent limitations reflect the designs researchers have concentrated on.

The authors articulate six positions spanning algorithms, systems, and evaluation. They revisit estimator-focused approaches through variance control, tradeoffs between variance and query count, and directional derivatives. They then highlight subspace and spectral approaches as opportunities to reduce variance with more favorable query scaling, broadening the design space beyond full-space, element-by-element estimation.

The paper also treats forward-only computation as a potential systems advantage for communication, pipelining, and training under resource constraints. It calls for evaluations that make the contribution of task complexity clearer. Together, these arguments motivate a research agenda built around zeroth-order methods’ distinctive strengths. The claimed opportunity is a viable path toward larger-scale, resource-efficient learning, rather than a blanket performance guarantee.
icml-2026-position-zeroth-order-optimiza.tldr: The authors argue that broader algorithmic and systems designs could unlock underexplored strengths of zeroth-order optimization.
